subtopics: C# as a compiled, strongly typed language
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of what is c#? in a C#/.NET program.

content.intro: What Is C#? is lesson 2 in Introduction to C#. C# is a statically typed, general-purpose language in the .NET ecosystem. The compiler checks program structure and types before execution.
content.why_it_matters: A language becomes useful when you can connect syntax to the tools that compile, run, and package an application. This lesson focuses on what is c#? and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: C# is a statically typed, general-purpose language in the .NET ecosystem. The compiler checks program structure and types before execution.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for what is c#?. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Key characteristics of C#
items.text: C# is statically typed: declared or inferred types constrain the operations available to a value, and compiler diagnostics can catch many type mismatches before execution.

items.title: C# as a compiled, strongly typed language
items.text: Separate source diagnostics, emitted assembly artifacts, and runtime execution; they are different stages with different failure modes.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates what is c#?. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates what is c#? rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for what is c#? before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
